children: Is Nebius
a buy, hold, or sell right now?
Seeking Alpha analysts
, and Dmitri Vinokurov weigh in.
Bay Area Ideas: Despite the mixed market sentiment for AI-related shares recently, I believe Nebius

is a clear buy. With the company scaling their capacity aggressively, hypergrowth has now been sustained for an extended period. Strong data center pricing dynamics and solid guidance indicate that tailwinds will continue for the foreseeable future.

For a neocloud that's scaling rapidly, the improvement in adjusted EBITDA margin is impressive, and the narrowing of adjusted net loss shows that management is focused on more than just top-line growth. In terms of the financial position, Nebius
shareholders have seen some dilution, but the conservative debt-to-equity ratio should allow them to withstand potential risks better than a company like CoreWeave
Lastly, I view the market's bearishness to Anthropic

CEO Dario Amodei's AI safety warnings as an overreaction. The odds of a development slowdown and weaker demand for Nebius's capacity are low. Washington and Beijing clearly have no interest in decelerating progress, so restrictive regulations are more than likely off the table.
Louis Gerard: I have been bearish on the firm for a long time now, and my answer is a Sell, as you might not be surprised considering my past ratings.
The business keeps on firing on all cylinders as Q2 revenue came to $582M, up 454% year-over-year, and contracted backlog sits near $40B, anchored by Meta
and Microsoft
, which are some of the best customers you would want to have.

But my problem is what sits underneath the firm as depreciation and amortization of $259.7M exceeded adjusted EBITDA of $236.2M in Q2, on a five-year server life assumption that I don’t think reflects the truth, especially when considering the pace of release of Nvidia
that happens every year.

Convertibles now stand at roughly $15B across eight series after August's $5.75B raise, and the August annual general meeting handed the board authority to issue another 20% of share capital without the need to ask for permission for five years. At roughly a $63B EV, you are paying about 20x the midpoint of 2026 revenue guidance. CEO Arkady Volozh himself gave the current pricing power a short window of between 18 and 24 months at recent conferences this month, and he is the CEO of NBIS, so not a doomsayer.
The Palantir
partnership is a genuine win, but it came with no disclosed total contract value, no committed capacity, and no revenue minimum, which is almost pointless at this stage. CoreWeave
and IREN
carry the same depreciation math. If you want the AI compute trade, Nvidia
gets you the economics without the refinancing calendar.
Nebius
isn't a bad company. It's a good company financed like a leveraged bet on prices its own CEO says have two years left.
Yiannis Zourmpanos: Nebius

remains a strong buy for me because the thesis keeps getting stronger: explosive AI cloud growth, $7-9B ARR guidance, rapidly expanding powered capacity, resilient pricing, and customer prepayments that improve funding economics.
Customer prepayments and infrastructure-backed financing are improving the capital equation. The Palantir
partnership adds enterprise distribution and sovereign AI credibility, while Nvidia
alignment strengthens Nebius across the AI stack.
Most importantly, Nebius

is evolving beyond renting GPUs toward a full-stack AI infrastructure platform spanning compute, inference, and software. I still think the market underestimates what happens if capacity, utilization, and revenue per megawatt keep scaling together.
Dmitri Vinokurov: Nebius's
recent price hikes on "on-demand," short-term GPU rentals are a testament to the enormous demand coming out of this space, with prices rising by around 20% on many Nvidia
GPUs.
Nebius
has leaned further into this space than competitors like CoreWeave
and IREN
by deliberately carving out capacity for these deals, a strong signal of their conviction that pricing stays elevated.

Some investors argue that exposure to short-term contracts trades cash-flow safety for extra revenue. But I'd turn the question back on them: if you're truly bullish on GPU pricing staying firm, not just for the next few quarters, but for at least the next two to three years, wouldn't you also want to capture this demand in the interim? Why lock in revenue now and leave money on the table?

Ultimately, neocloud investors are banking on three things: robust hyperscaler capex, strong GPU residual values, and a firm pricing environment. All three are firing on all cylinders right now, with no signs of slowing. I see Nebius
growing into a major player alongside the hyperscalers by 2030, and I remain bullish on both the company and the broader space as a whole.
